title: High Tight Flag
teaches: The high tight flag as we trade it: a quiet, liquid leader nearly doubles in a few weeks on a real change, pauses a few weeks a little under the high on lighter volume with tight closes, the buy is the trade through the pattern high at market, the stop sits a few cents under the day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: First, a stock must gain 100% to 120% in a span of four to eight weeks.

walkthroughs.title: SRPT, June 2015: the textbook pole and flag
steps: SRPT, 2015. A report, then a +60% day tops a near-vertical two-week run: +129% in 14 sessions.
Then a 14-day sideways flag, 15.0% deep, on lighter volume. It holds the 21-day EMA. The pattern high is the line.
2015-06-10: it trades through the high. Buy at market, 27.50. Stop a few cents under the day's low, 26.59.
Failure mode: a breakout nobody buys, stopped next session. Instead 3R comes on day 5. Time for the first sell.

walkthroughs.title: SOFI, November 2024: a gap over the high
steps: SOFI, 2024. The pole holds a report: +91% in 28 sessions. Then a 7-day flag, 9.9% deep.
The pattern high is 14.44. The stock gaps over it. The open is 1.5% past the high, inside the 4% line.
So the fill is the open, 14.65, at market. The stop sits under the day's low, 14.24: 2.8% of risk.
Failure mode: a close back under the high, stop taken next day. Instead 3R comes on day 3.

walkthroughs.title: BIDU, February 2021: trims, then the trail
steps: BIDU, 2021. A large-cap double, +100% in 36 sessions. A 12-day flag, 13.2% deep, on lighter volume.
2021-02-05: buy at market as it clears the high, 264.95. Stop under the day's low, 255.06.
3R on day 2: we hold. The first sell comes later, by judgment. It runs to about 354.
Failure mode: it unwinds as fast as it rose. Under the flag low by late March. The trail got you out.

questions.q: In one line, what is a high tight flag?
choices: A short rest after a near-double
A long box after a modest run
Pullbacks that keep shrinking
A sharp rebound off a crash low
questions.answer: A short rest after a near-double
questions.why: A short rest after a near-double. A quiet, liquid stock nearly doubles, then pauses a few weeks a little under its high. IBD: a gain of 100% to 120% in four to eight weeks. Then a pullback over the next three to five weeks. Bulkowski says it usually looks like a pause in the price rise, not a neat flag.
questions.lesson_line: A high tight flag is a rocket catching its breath for a few weeks, a little under the high.

wrong.A long box after a modest run: That is a flat base. The flag follows a far bigger, faster run and pauses for weeks, not months.
wrong.Pullbacks that keep shrinking: That is a VCP. The flag is one shelf a little under the high of the pole.
wrong.A sharp rebound off a crash low: That is a V. Bulkowski says to avoid V shapes, where price drops hard into the start of the pole.

questions.simple: A short pause after a near-double, because the stock rests near its high after a fast, huge run.

reasons: the exact pole size differs by source (IBD 100% to 120%, Bulkowski 90%) and is a held decision, so the key avoids it

questions.q: On a high tight flag the stop goes at the flag's low.
questions.why: False. The flag low is the line that kills the idea, not the stop. The stop sits a few cents under the entry day's low or the prior day's low.
questions.lesson_line: The flag low kills the idea. The day's low is the stop.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We buy at market as price trades above the peak of the ___.
questions.why: The pole. We buy at market as price trades through the pattern high, which is usually the top of the pole. IBD: the breakout clears the peak of the flagpole. Bulkowski: buy above the highest high in the pattern, usually the flagpole top. Our card adds: at least a cent over the high, regular hours only.
questions.lesson_line: The buy is above the top of the whole pattern, usually the pole's peak.
questions.simple: The pole, because we buy as price trades through the top of the run, the highest point of the whole pattern.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (entries are market orders, E57)
trigger choices are a held decision (D-027) but the key is the default every option keeps

questions.q: On our card, a proper flag's volume runs heavier than the pole's.
questions.why: False. On our card, flag volume runs below the pole's average. IBD: volume generally dries up. Bulkowski: it recedes through the flag for best performance.
questions.lesson_line: Loud on the way up, quiet in the flag. Holders are not selling.
questions.simple: False, because a proper flag is quiet, with volume lighter than it was on the pole.

reasons: the gate (below the pole's average) is a card proposal, not an owner ruling

questions.q: Where does the best pole usually start?
choices: A quiet base, then a real change
A crash low, then a rebound
A third leg in a huge run
A slow slide to lower lows
questions.answer: A quiet base, then a real change
questions.why: A quiet base, then a real change. Kuhn: the stock first sits in a well-contained base for months or years. Then an important news event usually lifts it out of dormancy. Bulkowski: poles springing from flat bases work better, and V shapes should be avoided. Our card grades a real change like earnings or a contract best.
questions.lesson_line: A sleeper that wakes up on news is the start you want, not a crash bounce.

wrong.A crash low, then a rebound: That is the V Bulkowski says to avoid: price drops hard into the start of the pole.
wrong.A third leg in a huge run: Late legs break down. Our card wants the first or second big leg, and Bonde says a tight flag late in the move breaks down.
wrong.A slow slide to lower lows: Kuhn describes a well-contained base first, not a slide.

questions.simple: A quiet base, then a real change, because a sleeper that wakes up for a reason starts a real pole.

deeper.example: SRPT, 2015. A +60% day on 2015-05-20, after the 2015-05-07 report, topped a near-vertical two-week run. Seven of the ten examples on our card had a report inside the pole.

reasons: the context cue is a card proposal, not an owner ruling
Kuhn's page is a publisher store page with only the opening paragraphs public

questions.q: Bulkowski says a high tight flag often does not look like a flag at all.
questions.why: True. Bulkowski: a high and tight flag is often not a flag at all. It usually looks like a pause in the price rise, not a flag or pennant. IBD says the action looks tight next to the steep run-up before it. So do not hunt for a neat shape. Look for a pause a little under the pole high.
questions.lesson_line: Do not hunt for a neat flag shape. Look for a pause that holds near the high.
questions.simple: True, because Bulkowski says it is often just a pause in the price rise, not a neat flag shape.

reasons: both Bulkowski quotes come from one author

questions.q: IBD says how many of these you might spot, if you are lucky?
choices: One or two in a bull market
A handful of new ones each month
About one new one every week
Two dozen in a bull market
questions.answer: One or two in a bull market
questions.why: One or two, if you are lucky. IBD, quoted by Bonde: you may spot one or two in a bull market. Bonde adds that finding too many means your reading is wrong. Our own scan found only 12 liquid hits in 36 years before 2020. Seeing one every week means ordinary flags are getting this name.
questions.lesson_line: If you see one every week, you are calling ordinary flags by the wrong name.

wrong.A handful of new ones each month: Too many. Bonde: if you find too many high tight flags, your reading is wrong.
wrong.About one new one every week: Far too many. Bonde: it is rare, and seeing too many means a misreading.
wrong.Two dozen in a bull market: Far too many. Our scan found only 12 liquid hits in 36 years before 2020.

questions.simple: One or two, because the pattern is rare and finding many means you are misreading it.

reasons: a count that can change (12 hits in 36 years comes from our own scan of today's tickers)
IBD's words are second-hand through Bonde

questions.q: A 30% run followed by a very tight flag counts as a high tight flag.
questions.why: False. Measure the pole first. A tight flag in a leader that never doubled is a bull flag, however tight. A high tight flag follows a near-double. A bull flag follows a much smaller run. The pole names the setup, not the tightness.
questions.lesson_line: The pole names the setup. Tightness alone never does.
questions.simple: False, because a 30% run never doubled, so even a very tight flag after it is a bull flag.

deeper.example: TSLA, 2023-07-14. A tight 8-day flag, 6.7% deep, on 0.78x volume. But the pole was 78% in 40 sessions, so it never doubled. A tight flag in a leader that never doubled is a bull flag, however tight. Best 1.88R, then stopped.

reasons: rests on the card's lookalike rule (single source)
the exact pole size is a held decision (D-048), but 30% fails every option

questions.q: How do we measure the flag's depth?
choices: Pattern high to flag low, on price
As a share of the pole's whole height
From the first flag close to the last
From the pole's low to the flag low
questions.answer: Pattern high to flag low, on price
questions.why: On price: the pattern's highest high down to the flag's lowest low, divided by that high. Kuhn measures against the advance, the pole's height. That gives a bigger number for the same flag. Kuhn's 10% to 20% limit is of the advance, so it is not the same yardstick.
questions.lesson_line: Depth is high to low on price. Measure it; do not eyeball it.

wrong.As a share of the pole's whole height: That is Kuhn's way, on the advance. It gives a bigger number for the same flag, so it is a different yardstick from price.
wrong.From the first flag close to the last: That is drift, not depth. Depth runs from the highest high to the lowest low.
wrong.From the pole's low to the flag low: That counts the whole run up as well. Depth is only the pullback, from the high down to the flag low.

questions.simple: We measure depth on price, from the pattern high down to the flag low, not as a share of the pole.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-050, flag depth)
fixed before

questions.q: Do the closes pass our tightness test?
questions.story: A stock doubled in five weeks after an earnings beat. It now pauses nine sessions under the high. The last five closes sit 8% apart.
choices: Yes, within 10% of each other
No, they must sit within 5%
No, they must sit within 1%
Yes, but only with light volume
questions.why: Yes. In the last 5 sessions before the trigger, the highest close must be no more than 10% above the lowest. These sit 8% apart, so they pass. Volume has its own separate line.
questions.lesson_line: Five closes within 10% of each other pass. Volume has its own line.

wrong.No, they must sit within 1%: Our line is 10%, not 1%. Closes 8% apart pass.
wrong.No, they must sit within 5%: Our line is 10%. Closes 8% apart are inside it.
wrong.Yes, but only with light volume: Volume is graded on its own line. The tightness test looks at closes only.

questions.simple: Yes, because the last five closes sit 8% apart, inside our 10% line.

deeper.trap: The trap is the stricter line. A limit of 1% or 5% sounds more careful, but ours is wider. The highest close in the last 5 sessions is no more than 10% above the lowest.

reasons: the 10% closes line is a card proposal, not an owner ruling
rests on one card line (c09)

questions.q: Before the entry, a close below the flag's low ends the setup.
questions.why: True. A close below the flag's low before entry ends the setup. The flag low is the line that kills the idea, so you wait for a new setup.
questions.lesson_line: Under the flag low, the idea is dead. Wait for a new setup.
questions.simple: True, because a close under the flag's low means the idea is dead, so you wait for a new setup.

reasons: rests on the card only (single source, c16)

questions.q: Which flag top grades best?
choices: A top that is flat or slopes down
A top that climbs a little each day
A top full of loose, wide swings
A top that sags to the pole low
questions.answer: A top that is flat or slopes down
questions.why: A top that is flat or slopes down. Our card calls a down-sloping or flat top on the flag the A+ shape. Bulkowski: flags with a down-sloping top trendline tend to outperform. TraderLion says the same, with no statistics. Bulkowski also says to trade tight flags, not loose ones.
questions.lesson_line: Flat or sloping down is the A+ shape. A rising top is not.

wrong.A top that climbs a little each day: Our card names a flat or down-sloping top the A+ shape. A top that keeps climbing is not that shape.
wrong.A top full of loose, wide swings: Bulkowski: trade tight flags, not loose ones.
wrong.A top that sags to the pole low: That gives back the whole run. Our flag is a pause a little under the pole high.

questions.simple: A flat or down-sloping top, because our card grades it A+ and Bulkowski says down-sloping tops tend to outperform.

reasons: the flat-top half rests on the card only; Bulkowski and TraderLion speak of down-sloping tops
TraderLion's page could not be fetched live, so it only supports

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A trade still under 1R after ___ trading days is sold.
questions.why: 10 trading days. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. It counts trading days, not calendar days. A trade at 1R or better is not caught by this rule.
questions.lesson_line: Give it two weeks to pay. Under 1R by then, it goes.
questions.simple: After 10 trading days, a trade still under 1R is sold so the money is free.

deeper.counter: TMDX took 23 sessions to reach 3R, but it was above 1R by day 10. The time stop sells only trades still under 1R, so TMDX would have been kept.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: Once you are filled, a real stop order goes in with the broker straight away.
questions.why: True. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. It goes in at once after the fill. It only moves up, never down or wider.
questions.lesson_line: Filled, then the stop goes in at once. Never a stop kept in your head.
questions.simple: True. A real stop order goes in with the broker as soon as you are filled.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D41, A4)

questions.q: What flag volume makes the A grade on our card?
choices: 60% of the pole's volume or less
About 80% of the pole's volume
A bit above the pole's volume
Any volume below the pole's
questions.answer: 60% of the pole's volume or less
questions.why: 60% of the pole's volume or less is the A grade on our card. Any flag volume below the pole's average passes the gate, and the lighter the better. IBD: volume generally dries up. Bulkowski: it recedes for best performance.
questions.lesson_line: Quieter flag, better grade. Under the pole's volume is the floor.

wrong.About 80% of the pole's volume: That passes the gate but grades below A. The A grade is at most 60% of the pole's.
wrong.A bit above the pole's volume: That is above the pole's average, so it fails the gate.
wrong.Any volume below the pole's: That is the gate, the pass line. The A grade needs 60% of the pole's or less.

questions.simple: 60% of the pole's volume or less, because our card gives the A grade to the quietest flags.

deeper.example: CRNC, December 2020. Flag volume ran 0.95x the pole's, barely under it. That passes the gate, but it is only a B on this line.

reasons: the 60% A-grade line is a card proposal that can change
rests on one card line (c08)

questions.q: Which stop is ours on a high tight flag?
choices: A few cents under the entry day's low
Just under the flag's lowest low
A flat 8% below the price you paid
One average day's range under entry
questions.answer: A few cents under the entry day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the entry day's low, or under the prior day's low. Stop first: the size comes from the stop. It usually sits within about 3% of the buy and only moves up. The flag low is the line that kills the idea, not the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, a few cents under the day's low. Then the size.

wrong.Just under the flag's lowest low: That is Bulkowski's stop. For us the flag low kills the idea but is not the stop. His study of a penny under the flag low averaged a 26% loss.
wrong.A flat 8% below the price you paid: That is IBD's 8% sell rule, not our stop. It triggered on Taser, which then regained the buy point.
wrong.One average day's range under entry: Kullamagi uses the average range only as a cap on width. Our stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

questions.simple: Our stop sits a few cents under the entry day's low, close to the buy, because the stop sets the size.

deeper.counter: Bulkowski's automated study found that a penny under the flag low as a stop meant an average 26% loss. Our stop is far tighter. The flag low ends the idea but does not set the stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)

questions.q: You are in, and the breakout day ends on light volume. That alone is a reason to sell before the stop.
questions.why: False. Light breakout volume grades the trade, but it is not a reason to exit. After the entry, the stop is the exit, with the time stop and the trail.
questions.lesson_line: Once you are in, the stop decides. Not the volume bar.
questions.simple: False, because light volume only grades the trade and the stop is the exit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop is the exit)

questions.q: Bulkowski's measure rule adds half the pole to the flag low. What is it for us?
choices: A reference, not a sell rule
Our target; sell it all there
A level to add more shares
Where the first third comes off
questions.answer: A reference, not a sell rule
questions.why: A reference, not a sell rule. Bulkowski's measure adds half the pole to the flag low, and 82% of his perfect trades met it. We have no price target. The first sell is a judgment, not a projected price, and the rest rides the trail.
questions.lesson_line: We sell on judgment and by the trail, never by a projected target.

wrong.Our target; sell it all there: We have no price target. The sells are a judgment and the rest rides the trail.
wrong.A level to add more shares: We never add to a trade. The full size goes in at one price with one stop.
wrong.Where the first third comes off: The first sell is a judgment, not a projected price from the measure rule.

questions.simple: It is only a reference. We sell on judgment and by the trail, not at a projected price.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)

questions.q: On a high tight flag our hard rule sells the first third at 3R.
questions.why: False. There is no hard rule for the first sell. It is a judgment. He very rarely sells on day 1 of the buy and usually waits until day 3 at the earliest. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third. Wait for the push.
questions.simple: False. The first sell is a judgment, usually no earlier than day 3, not a fixed third at 3R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)

questions.q: Bought at 27.50 with the stop at 26.59. Where is 3R?
questions.why: One R is the fill minus the stop, 27.50 minus 26.59. Add three of those to the fill: 27.50 plus 3 times (27.50 minus 26.59) is 30.23. 3R is a yardstick, not an automatic sale. SRPT got there on day 5.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. It is a yardstick, not an automatic sale.
questions.simple: Add three times the risk per share to the fill, which puts 3R at 30.23.

deeper.trap: Do not add three times the fill. Add three times the gap between the fill and the stop.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)

wrong.$28.41: That adds one R, not three.
wrong.$29.32: That counts 3R up from the stop, not from the fill.
wrong.$31.14: That adds four R. Three R is three gaps, not four.

questions.q: What usually sits behind the pole?
choices: A real change in the business
A rally in the whole market
A stock split or a name change
A big index fund rebalance
questions.answer: A real change in the business
questions.why: A real change in the business, such as earnings, a product or a contract. With heavy volume it is the A+ context. Seven of the ten examples had a report inside the pole. Kuhn: a news event usually lifts the stock out of dormancy.
questions.lesson_line: Ask why it doubled. A real change in the business is the best answer.

wrong.A stock split or a name change: A split changes the share count, not the business. It is no reason to double.
wrong.A big index fund rebalance: Flows can move a stock, but the card's A+ context is a change in the business.
wrong.A rally in the whole market: A market-wide rally does not explain one quiet stock nearly doubling. The card says usually a real change in that company.

questions.simple: Usually a real change in the business, like earnings, a product or a contract, wakes a quiet stock.

reasons: rests on a proposed decision (D-007, catalyst grade)

questions.q: At the trigger, the close must be above the 200-day average.
questions.why: True. The close is above the 200-day simple moving average at the trigger. Our rule is no longs below the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: The close must be above the 200-day at the trigger. Below it, we pass.
questions.simple: True. We take no long below the 200-day average, so the close must be above it at the trigger.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: The lowest low of the 40 sessions was 12.40 and the pole high is 26.00. How far did price rise, in percent?
questions.why: The rise is the high over the low, minus one: 26.00 divided by 12.40, less one, is 109.7%. That is more than a double. Measure from the lowest low of the 40 sessions ending at the pole high. IBD looks for 100% to 120%. Bulkowski wants at least 90%.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the pole before you look at the flag.
questions.simple: The pole rose 109.7% from its low to its high, which is more than a double.

reasons: computed key
rests on a held decision (D-048, pole size)

wrong.209.7%: That forgets to take off one. It is the ratio, not the rise.
wrong.52.3%: That divides the rise by the high. Divide by the low, where it started.
wrong.13.6%: That is the dollar amount read as a percent. Divide it first.

questions.q: Pattern high 100.00, flag low 84.00. How deep is the flag, in percent?
questions.why: Depth is the pattern high minus the flag low, divided by the high: (100.00 minus 84.00) divided by 100.00 is 16%. IBD says the flag usually pulls back 10% to 20%, sometimes 25%.
questions.lesson_line: Depth is high to low on price, divided by the high.
questions.simple: Depth is the drop from the pattern high to the flag low as a share of the high, here 16%.

reasons: computed key
rests on a held decision (D-050, flag depth)

wrong.19.0%: That divides by the low. Depth is measured against the high.
wrong.84.0%: That is the low as a share of the high, not the drop.

questions.q: Fill 14.65, stop 14.24. How far below the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: Take the fill minus the stop and divide by the fill: (14.65 minus 14.24) divided by 14.65 is 2.8%. Our stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy. This was SOFI's stop.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: The stop is 2.8% under the 14.65 fill, which is inside the usual 3%.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A13)

wrong.0.4%: That is the dollar amount read as a percent. Divide it first.
wrong.97.2%: That is the stop as a share of the fill, not the gap.

questions.q: Bought at 264.95, stop 255.06. The stock trades to 314.40. How many R is that?
questions.why: The gain is 314.40 minus 264.95. One R is 264.95 minus 255.06. The gain divided by one R is 5.0. Selling at about 5 to 10R is often best, but the sell is a judgment. BIDU got there.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars. About 5R to 10R is often a good place to sell.
questions.simple: The gain is five times the risk per share, so the stock is up 5R.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (E51)

wrong.6.0R: That counts the gain from the stop, so it reads one R too high.
wrong.49.5R: That is the dollar gain read as R. Divide it by the risk per share.
wrong.0.2R: That divides the gain by the price, not by R.

questions.q: Account 100,000. Risk 0.5%. Fill 132.97, stop 128.10. How many shares?
questions.why: The risk budget is 0.5% of 100,000, which is 500. Divide it by the fill minus the stop, 132.97 minus 128.10, and round down. That gives 102 shares, the full size at one price with one stop.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size. Never the other way round.
questions.simple: Divide the 0.5% risk on 100,000 by the risk per share, then round down to 102 shares.

deeper.trap: Always round down, never up. Rounding up would risk more than the 0.5% you set. This size is also well under the 40% cap on one position.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A5)

choices: 500 shares
1,026 shares
102 shares
300 shares

wrong.1,026 shares: That risks ten times the budget. A decimal slip.
wrong.300 shares: That is the 40% position cap size. The stop gives a smaller size.
wrong.500 shares: That is the risk dollars read as shares. Divide by the risk per share.

questions.q: The 10-day average is 50.00. Above what price is a buy too stretched?
questions.why: Skip a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average. 10% over 50.00 is 50.00 times 1.10, or 55.00. About 5% over the average is the A+ zone, and 8% to 10% is B-.
questions.lesson_line: Read the stretch in percent before you read the pattern.
questions.simple: The limit is 10% over the 10-day average, and 10% over 50.00 is 55.00.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (C29)
fixed before

wrong.$60.50: Took the 10 percent twice, one on top of the other.
wrong.$550.00: Decimal slip: ten times too big.

questions.q: Buy the open, or pass?
questions.story: The pattern high is 60.00 and your alert sits there. News hits overnight. The stock opens at 63.30.
choices: Pass; past the 4% line
Buy; the breakout is real
Buy half size at the open
Pass; any gap is skipped
questions.why: Pass. We never buy more than 4% above the pattern high, and a gap over it by more than 4% is skipped. The open at 63.30 is past that line from 60.00. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink. A gap that stays inside 4% is still bought at the open.
questions.lesson_line: I would rather miss it than chase it. Four percent and done.

wrong.Buy; the breakout is real: Real and too far away are both true. The chase line is 4%.
wrong.Buy half size at the open: Half of a bad entry is still a bad entry.
wrong.Pass; any gap is skipped: A gap that stays inside 4% is still bought at the open. SOFI's was, 1.5% past the high.

questions.simple: Pass, because the open is more than 4% above the pattern high and we never chase past that line.

deeper.trap: The alert fires at the pattern high, so the move feels like one you already own. The 4% line is measured from the pattern high, not from your alert or the news. A gap that stays inside it is still bought at the open: SOFI opened 1.5% past the high and was bought.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, no chasing)

questions.q: Buy the break today, and why?
questions.story: The pole came off a report. The flag is 12 sessions old and tight. The next report is in 2 sessions.
choices: No; the report is too close
No; the flag is too young
Yes; the flag is tight enough
Yes, and sell before the report
questions.answer: No; the report is too close
questions.why: No. We take no new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report, and this report is 2 sessions away. A tight flag does not change the calendar. Check the date every time: the pole often follows a report, and the next one can land inside the flag.
questions.lesson_line: Check the report date every time. Inside 3 sessions, wait.

wrong.Yes, and sell before the report: The rule is no new buy inside the window, not a quick trip in and out.
wrong.No; the flag is too young: A 12-session flag fits our card, which allows 5 to 30 sessions. The report is the problem.
wrong.Yes; the flag is tight enough: A tight flag does not change the calendar. The window comes first.

questions.simple: No. A report is 2 sessions away, and we take no new buys in the 3 sessions before one.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)
fixed before

questions.q: What is your stop now?
questions.story: Bought at 52.00, stop 51.00. Bad news overnight: it opens at 50.40. The first 5-minute bar's low is 50.25 and the first 30-minute bar's low is 50.10.
choices: The low of the first 30-minute bar
Sell at the open price of 50.40
The flag's low, to give it room
The low of the first 5-minute bar
questions.answer: The low of the first 30-minute bar
questions.why: The low of the first 30-minute bar, 50.10, is the new stop. On a gap against the stop, the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The loss to that low is under twice your starting risk, so it is inside the 2R ceiling. Past 2R, you get out.
questions.lesson_line: On a gap through the stop, let the first 30 minutes set the new stop.

wrong.Sell at the open price of 50.40: Our gap rule lets the first 30 minutes decide, with a ceiling at 2R. It does not say to sell at the open.
wrong.The flag's low, to give it room: That widens the stop. The gap rule is the one exception, and it uses the 30-minute low.
wrong.The low of the first 5-minute bar: The gap rule uses the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day. A 5-minute bar is a different line.

questions.simple: Use the low of the first 30-minute bar as the new stop, because the gap rule lets those 30 minutes decide.

deeper.trap: Check the ceiling first. If the first 30-minute bar's low were far lower, so the loss passed 2R, you would get out instead of holding.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)
fixed before

questions.q: A wicky breakout bar that closes well off its high grades lower than a strong close.
questions.why: True. A strong close on the breakout day raises the grade. A wicky bar that closes off its high is B-. It is a grade cue on our card, so where the day closes counts.
questions.lesson_line: Where the breakout day closes tells you who won the day.
questions.simple: True, because a strong close on the breakout day raises the grade, while a bar closing off its high is a B-.

deeper.example: FSLR, 2022-08-26. The breakout day gapped open at 125.50, over the 121.91 buy point, on 1.47x volume. It then closed at the low of its range, 121.75, back under the buy point. That is a weak close, the opposite of the strong close that raises the grade.

reasons: rests on the card only (single source, c31)
a house grading line, not a web fact

questions.q: Widen the stop, hold it, or sell?
questions.story: Four days after the breakout the stock drifts back to the pattern high. Your stop has not been touched.
choices: Hold; the stop is the exit
Widen it to the flag low
Sell now, before it fails
Add more at the pattern high
questions.answer: Hold; the stop is the exit
questions.why: Hold. After the entry, the stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. A pullback to the pattern high is not a signal to sell early, widen the stop or add.
questions.lesson_line: Until the stop is hit, the plan holds. The stop is the answer, not your nerves.

wrong.Widen it to the flag low: The stop never moves down. Widening it is the mistake the rule exists to stop.
wrong.Sell now, before it fails: The stop has not been hit, and the stop is the exit. Selling early swaps the plan for nerves.
wrong.Add more at the pattern high: We never add. The full size goes on at one price with one stop.

questions.simple: Hold, because the stop is the exit and it has not been touched.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop only moves up)
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: What does the time stop say?
questions.story: Ten trading days after the breakout, the trade is up 1.3R. It is grinding higher, not running.
choices: Keep it; it is over 1R
Sell; it has not reached 3R
Keep it, and add a little more
Move the stop to the flag low
questions.why: Keep it. The time stop sells a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days. This one is up 1.3R, so it is over the line. Slow is not a reason to sell. TMDX took 23 sessions to 3R but was above 1R by day 10.
questions.lesson_line: Slow is not wrong. Under 1R after ten days is the line.

wrong.Sell; it has not reached 3R: The time stop is 1R after ten days, not 3R.
wrong.Move the stop to the flag low: The stop only moves up. The flag low is below it.
wrong.Keep it, and add a little more: We never add. The full size goes on at one price with one stop.

questions.simple: Keep it, because the time stop only sells a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C33, time stop)

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
questions.story: Bought at 40.00, stop 39.00, so 3R is 43.00. The next morning it opens at 43.60.
choices: No rule forces a sale; use judgment
Sell one third at the open by rule
Sell the whole lot at the open
Wait for a dip back to 43.00
questions.answer: No rule forces a sale; use judgment
questions.why: No rule forces a sale. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. He very rarely sells on day 1 of the buy and usually waits until day 3 at the earliest. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past 3R forces no sale. The first sell is a judgment.

wrong.Wait for a dip back to 43.00: There is no rule to wait for a dip either. Judge the push on its own.
wrong.Sell the whole lot at the open: That sells the whole position at once. The first sell is a judgment and the rest rides the trail.
wrong.Sell one third at the open by rule: 3R is not a fixed sale point. The first sell is a judgment, not a rule.

questions.simple: No rule forces a sale at the open. The first sell is a judgment, usually no earlier than day 3.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F63, trim at the open)
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: The first third is off at 3R. Where does our default put the stop?
choices: To breakeven, your fill price
Leave it under the entry day
Down to the flag low for room
Up to the 3R price you sold at
questions.why: To breakeven, your fill price. Our default moves the stop to breakeven at the first trim. The allowed window is 2R to 5R, ideally. Leaving the stop where it was is not the default. The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
questions.lesson_line: First trim, then breakeven. The rest of the trade is free.

wrong.Leave it under the entry day: At the first trim our default moves it up to breakeven.
wrong.Down to the flag low for room: A stop never moves down or wider.
wrong.Up to the 3R price you sold at: The default at the first trim is breakeven, not the trim price.

questions.simple: Move the stop to your fill price, because our default is breakeven at the first trim.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, breakeven window and default)
+1 reworded: the old stem allowed a second answer

questions.q: This stock trades 3,000,000 shares a day. The most you would own?
choices: 30,000 shares, 1% of a day
300,000 shares, 10% of a day
As many as the risk size allows
No limit if the stop is tight
questions.why: 30,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 3,000,000 is 30,000. The rule has no exception for a tight stop. Illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume is the ceiling, however tight the stop.

wrong.300,000 shares, 10% of a day: That is ten times the 1% line.
wrong.As many as the risk size allows: The risk-based size is only one limit. We also never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.
wrong.No limit if the stop is tight: The rule says never, with no exception for a tight stop.

questions.simple: We own at most 1% of the average daily volume, and 1% of 3,000,000 is 30,000 shares.

reasons: one cited fact only
computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

questions.q: Take it or pass?
questions.story: The stock doubled in six weeks and now flags tight. It trades at 8.40, about $35 million a day.
choices: Pass; it is under the $10 floor
Take it; the dollar volume is fine
Take it at half size to limit risk
Pass; the double came too fast
questions.answer: Pass; it is under the $10 floor
questions.why: Pass. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. At 8.40 this one fails the price test, even though $35 million a day clears the volume test. Both tests must pass. Bonde: some hits are too low priced and need liquidity.
questions.lesson_line: Cheap and thin is not ours, however good the chart.

wrong.Take it; the dollar volume is fine: Both tests apply: $10 or more and $20 million a day. Price fails.
wrong.Take it at half size to limit risk: The floor is a gate, not a size cue.
wrong.Pass; the double came too fast: A double in four to eight weeks is the pole this pattern needs. Six weeks is not too fast.

questions.simple: Pass, because the stock trades under $10 and we only trade stocks at $10 or more.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B23, price and dollar volume floor)

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: A clean flag sets up after a double. The market reading has been Red for two weeks. Most leaders are breaking down.
choices: Pass; this market says wait
Pass; the flag is too tight
Buy full size; the chart is A+
Buy a starter; add on strength
questions.why: Pass. The market reading is a guide. Green is full risk, Yellow smaller and fewer, Orange only A+ setups, Red mostly cash and shorts. In Red a long mostly waits, however clean the flag. Bulkowski: if the market looks about to drop, avoid the trade.
questions.lesson_line: The market first, then the chart. A great flag in a Red market waits.

wrong.Buy full size; the chart is A+: Red is mostly cash. Even Orange takes only A+ setups, and this is Red.
wrong.Pass; the flag is too tight: A tight flag is what we want. The market reading is the reason to wait.
wrong.Buy a starter; add on strength: We never add. And Red is not the time to start.

questions.simple: Pass, because a Red market reading means mostly cash and shorts, however good the chart looks.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F65, the market reading as a guide)

questions.q: What relative strength do we want on this setup?
choices: An RS rating of 80 or more
A rating over 50 will do
RS is not a factor here
A rating of 99 or better
questions.answer: An RS rating of 80 or more
questions.why: An RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. We buy leaders. IBD gave Taser a 98 RS grade at its breakout.
questions.lesson_line: Buy leaders. An RS rating of 80 or more is the floor.

wrong.RS is not a factor here: Buy leaders is our rule on every long setup except parabolic and mean-reversion trades.
wrong.A rating of 99 or better: Too narrow. Our floor is 80, not 99.

questions.simple: We want an RS rating of 80 or more, because we buy leaders.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C31, RS 80 or more)
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: A VCP is one shelf a little under the high; a high tight flag strings shrinking pullbacks.
questions.why: False. The two are swapped. A VCP strings two to six contractions over 15 sessions or more after a 30% advance. A high tight flag is one shelf a little under the high of a near-double pole.
questions.lesson_line: Several shrinking dips is a VCP. One shelf after a rocket is the flag.
questions.simple: False. A VCP strings shrinking pullbacks, while a high tight flag is one shelf after a huge run.

reasons: one cited fact only

questions.q: Take it or pass?
questions.story: The stock was up 250% in the six months before this pole began. Now it doubles again and pauses tight.
choices: Pass; it is too late in the move
Pass; a tight flag is a trap
Take it; a fresh first base
Take it; momentum makes it A+
questions.answer: Pass; it is too late in the move
questions.why: Pass. Our not-late test: the pole is the first or second big leg. The stock must not be up more than 200% in the 6 months before the pole began. This one was up 250%. Bonde: if a tight flag appears late in the move, it will break down. Tight does not fix a late flag.
questions.lesson_line: Early legs pay. A flag after a giant run is where tired moves end.

wrong.Pass; a tight flag is a trap: Bulkowski: trade tight flags, not loose ones. Tight is not the problem; the 250% run before the pole is.
wrong.Take it; a fresh first base: Our card wants the first or second big leg. A stock already up 250% in six months is not a fresh first base.
wrong.Take it; momentum makes it A+: Momentum this late is the risk, not the edge. The not-late line is a gate: no more than 200% up in the 6 months before the pole.

questions.simple: Pass, because the stock was already up 250% in six months, past our 200% limit, so the move is late.

deeper.trap: The trap is momentum. A stock up 250% in six months that doubles again looks strong, so the flag feels earned. Our test looks backward instead: no more than 200% up in the 6 months before the pole began. Past that line, Bonde says a tight flag late in the move breaks down.

reasons: the 200% in 6 months line is a card proposal that can change
Bonde's late-flag point comes from one post

questions.q: Which entry did Bulkowski find fails too often on this pattern?
choices: A trendline break in the flag
A trade above the highest high
A buy at the next day's open
A close above the pole top
questions.answer: A trendline break in the flag
questions.why: A trendline break in the flag. Bulkowski: new research says high and tight flags fail too often on a flag trendline break, so place a buy stop above the highest high in the pattern. A close above its highest peak, usually the pole top, confirms the pattern. We buy at market as price trades through the pattern high.
questions.lesson_line: Never buy the line inside the flag. Buy the top of the pattern.

wrong.A trade above the highest high: That is the entry he recommends, and ours: through the pattern high.
wrong.A buy at the next day's open: That is a timing choice. His warning is about the trendline break inside the flag.
wrong.A close above the pole top: He uses a close above the top to confirm the pattern, not to reject it.

questions.simple: Buying a trendline break inside the flag fails too often, so buy above the highest high of the pattern instead.

deeper.trap: Some chart vendors teach an early entry: buy when price breaks above the downward trendline inside the flag. It feels smarter because it is earlier. Bulkowski says too many of these patterns fail to move higher even after a trendline break, so the trigger is the pattern high, not the line inside the flag.

reasons: +2 Bulkowski's finding is new research and can change
+2 held decision D-027 (which trigger we use)
+1 fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: Pole low 10.00, pole high 20.00, flag low 17.00. Where is Bulkowski's reference level?
questions.why: Bulkowski: take half of the pole and add it to the bottom of the flag. The pole runs from 10.00 to 20.00, so half of it is (20.00 minus 10.00) divided by 2. Add that to the flag low: 17.00 plus that half is 22.00. His rule was met by 82% of his perfect trades. For us it is a reference only. We sell by R and the trail.
questions.lesson_line: Know the level if you like. It is never the reason to sell.
questions.simple: Half the pole added to the flag low lands at 22.00, which is a reference only.

reasons: +2 computed key

wrong.$15.00: That adds half the pole to the pole low, not to the flag low.
wrong.$17.00: That is the flag low. The half pole must be added.
wrong.$12.00: That takes half the pole off the flag low.

questions.q: High tight flag or bull flag?
questions.story: The stock ran 45% in three weeks on strong earnings. It paused six sessions in a tight range near the high.
choices: A bull flag
A high tight flag
A flat base
A VCP base
questions.why: A bull flag. Measure the pole: 45% is far short of a near-double. A tight flag in a leader that never doubled is a bull flag, however tight.
questions.lesson_line: Doubled and paused is the rare one. Ran and paused is the common flag.

wrong.A high tight flag: The card wants a near-double, 90% or more in 40 sessions or fewer. A 45% run is far short.
wrong.A flat base: A flat base rests at least 25 sessions. This one paused six sessions.
wrong.A VCP base: A VCP strings two to six contractions over 15 sessions or more. Six tight sessions is one short pause, not a string of shrinking dips.

questions.simple: It is a bull flag. The pole is only 45%, nowhere near a double, and tightness alone never makes a high tight flag.

deeper.trap: Do not let the tight box name the setup. Measure the pole first: a near-double is 90% or more in 40 sessions or fewer.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-048, pole size)
fixed before

questions.q: Which card do you grade it on?
questions.story: The stock doubled in seven weeks. Then it rested 38 sessions in a 9% box near the high.
choices: Flat base; the pause is too long
High tight flag; the price doubled
Bull flag; the box is tight
VCP; the base is quiet and tight
questions.answer: Flat base; the pause is too long
questions.why: The flat base. Count the rest. Our card allows a pause of 5 to 30 sessions, and past 30 the flag becomes that base. IBD gives three to five weeks, and Kuhn three to six. The double fits, but 38 sessions is too long.
questions.lesson_line: A flag rests a few weeks. A much longer rest is a different base, graded as that base.

wrong.High tight flag; the price doubled: The double fits, but the rest runs past 30 sessions. Past that, the flag has become a base.
wrong.Bull flag; the box is tight: A bull flag follows a smaller run, 20% to 30%. This stock doubled, and then it sat far longer than a flag does.
wrong.VCP; the base is quiet and tight: A VCP strings two to six contractions after a 30% advance. This is one 9% box with no string of dips.

questions.simple: It is a flat base, because past 30 sessions the flag has become a base.

deeper.trap: Count the rest in sessions. Our card allows 5 to 30. IBD gives three to five weeks and Kuhn three to six, so 38 sessions is past even Kuhn's longest flag.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-049, flag length)
fixed before

questions.q: Buy the pause, or not?
questions.story: The pole's last three days were all up days, each a gap up on rising volume and a wider range. The last one, the climax day, closed below its open. Now it pauses.
choices: Not; it reads as a parabolic top
Not; a gap means the move is over
Buy it; the pause is very tight
Buy over the climax day's high
questions.answer: Not; it reads as a parabolic top
questions.why: Not. The last leg of the pole was a burst: gap ups, rising volume and wider ranges. The climax day closed below its open. Our card calls that a possible parabolic top, not a flag. A pause afterward does not cancel the reversal.
questions.lesson_line: Read the last leg of the pole. A burst that reverses is a top, not a flag.

wrong.Buy over the climax day's high: The trigger is fine on a flag. This is not a flag.
wrong.Not; a gap means the move is over: Gaps alone do not end a move. SOFI gapped over its pattern high and ran to 6.2R. The warning is the climax day closing below its open.
wrong.Buy it; the pause is very tight: Tight does not cancel the reversal. The card calls it a possible top.

questions.simple: Not, because the pole ended in a burst and the climax day closed below its open, which marks a possible top.

deeper.trap: The trap is the tidy pause. A tight pause looks like a flag, so the eye skips the last leg. The card reads that leg first. A burst of gap ups, then a climax day that closed below its open, is a possible top. It is not a flag.

reasons: rests on the card's parabolic-top test only (c18, c42)
a proposed test, not an owner ruling

questions.q: Which card fits?
questions.story: The stock rose 35% in six weeks. Then it tightened for four weeks with higher lows, riding its rising short averages.
choices: The Qullamaggie breakout
High tight flag setup
A V off a crash low
A flat base or a cup
questions.why: The Qullamaggie breakout. It needs only a 30% move in the past 1 to 3 months and rests 2 weeks to 2 months. A high tight flag needs the double in 8 weeks or less. This stock rose 35% in six weeks, so it fits his breakout, not the near-double. His stock surfs the rising 10- and 20-day through the rest.
questions.lesson_line: The pole decides which card you are on.

wrong.High tight flag setup: 35% is nowhere near a double. The flag needs the near-double first.
wrong.A V off a crash low: Nothing here fell. It rose and tightened.
wrong.A flat base or a cup: A base that lost the fast averages is a flat base or a cup. This one rides its rising short averages.

questions.simple: The Qullamaggie breakout, because it needs only a 30% move, while the high tight flag needs a double.

deeper.trap: The trap is the shared look. Both end in a tight pause near the high, so the chart alone does not name the card. Measure the pole. His breakout needs a 30% move in the past 1 to 3 months. The high tight flag needs the double in 8 weeks or less.

reasons: the card's summary of his breakout; his page gives 30% to 100%+ in 1 to 3 months
the near-double size is a held decision (D-048), but 35% fails every option

questions.q: Take it or pass?
questions.story: The stock fell 45% in six weeks. Then it doubled off the low in five weeks and now pauses near the high.
choices: Pass; it is a V off a crash
Take it; the pole doubled
Take it; the flag is tight
Pass; the run was too fast
questions.answer: Pass; it is a V off a crash
questions.why: Pass. Not a V: in the 40 sessions before the pole began, the stock must not fall over 30% from high to low. This one fell 45% in six weeks, so the pole is a rebound off a crash. Bulkowski: avoid V shapes, where price drops hard into the start of the pole. He says poles springing from flat bases work better.
questions.lesson_line: A double off a crash is a repair, not a launch.

wrong.Take it; the pole doubled: The double is real, but it starts from a crash. That is the V the card rules out.
wrong.Take it; the flag is tight: A tight flag does not fix where the pole began.
wrong.Pass; the run was too fast: Speed is part of the pattern. The rise takes 40 sessions or fewer, and five weeks fits.

questions.simple: Pass, because the stock fell 45% before the pole began, which makes it a V off a crash, not a fresh launch.

deeper.trap: The trap is the double. A pole that doubles looks like the pattern, but a double off a crash low only repairs the damage. Check what came before it: in the 40 sessions before the pole began, a fall of more than 30% fails the test.

reasons: the 30% fall limit is a card proposal that can change
Bulkowski independently says to avoid V shapes

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You bought a stock that rose 291% in 34 sessions, then flagged six days. The breakout day traded a tenth of its average volume. Next morning it falls to your stop.
choices: Sell at the stop, as planned
Hold; the pole was huge
Widen the stop to the flag low
Buy more; it is cheaper
questions.answer: Sell at the stop, as planned
questions.why: Sell at the stop. After the entry, the stop is the exit, with the time stop and the trail. The stop only moves up, never down or wider. SRRK, December 2020: the biggest pole in the scan, 291% in 34 sessions, but the breakout day traded about a tenth of its average volume. It was stopped the next session. Light breakout volume grades the trade; it is not a reason to exit.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is an appointment, not a debate. Even after a perfect-looking pole.

wrong.Hold; the pole was huge: The size of the pole does not move the stop. The stop is the exit.
wrong.Widen the stop to the flag low: The stop only moves up. Widening it is the mistake.
wrong.Buy more; it is cheaper: We never add, least of all to a trade going through its stop.

questions.simple: Sell at the stop, because after the entry the stop is the exit and the size of the pole does not change that.

deeper.trap: A perfect-looking pole. 291% in 34 sessions was the biggest pole in our scan, and the flag was 6 days and 15.5% deep. None of that moves the stop. A pole is a reason to buy, never a reason to hold past the stop. The breakout day traded 0.10x its 50-day average, and light volume only grades the trade.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop is the exit)
+2 held decision D-006 (breakout volume as a gate)

questions.q: The next morning it takes your stop. Was buying the gap a mistake?
questions.story: A high tight flag passes every gate. The stock gaps open at 125.50 over the 121.91 buy point on 1.47x volume. You are filled. It closes at 121.75, the low of its day.
choices: No; a planned loss at the stop
Yes; skip gaps next time
No; but widen the stop next time
Yes; volume was too light
questions.answer: No; a planned loss at the stop
questions.why: No. A gap over the high that stays inside the 4% line is bought at the open, and the stop is the exit. The open at 125.50 was past the 121.91 buy point but inside that line. FSLR, August 2022: the next session's low, 118.13, took the stop. A loss at the stop is the system working.
questions.lesson_line: A loss at the stop is the cost of being there for the ones that work.

wrong.Yes; volume was too light: It broke out on 1.47x volume, well above average. The buy followed the rules, and the stop is the exit.
wrong.Yes; skip gaps next time: A gap over the high is bought at the open when it is inside 4%. SOFI was, and ran.
wrong.No; but widen the stop next time: Our stop sits a few cents under the day's low. A wider stop means fewer shares, not a better trade.

questions.simple: No, because a gap inside the 4% line is bought at the open, and a loss at the stop is a planned cost.

deeper.trap: Judging the trade by its result. The gap was bought by the rule, inside the 4% line, so the loss was a planned cost. The bar did close at the low of its day, back under the buy point, and a wicky bar that closes off its high grades B-. SOFI also gapped, 1.5% past the high, and reached 3R on day 3.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, 4% line; A4, the stop is the exit)

questions.q: Was the loss a mistake?
questions.story: Bought at 175.81, stop 168.86. It reaches 2.35R, then falls back. On day 3 it trades through your stop.
choices: No; the stop was the planned exit
No; but skip this stock next time
Yes; you should sell at 2R
Yes; widen the stop next time
questions.answer: No; the stop was the planned exit
questions.why: No. The stop is the exit, so the loss was planned. This trade topped out at 2.35R, and the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 at the earliest. Our rule also lets the stop go to breakeven anywhere from 2R to 5R, ideally. Had that been done at 2R, this would have been a scratch.
questions.lesson_line: A trade that reaches 2R and comes back is still a planned loss, or a scratch.

wrong.Yes; you should sell at 2R: No rule sells at 2R. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed level.
wrong.Yes; widen the stop next time: Our stop sits a few cents under the day's low. A wider stop means fewer shares, not a better trade.
wrong.No; but skip this stock next time: A stop-out is not a ban. After one, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

questions.simple: No, because the stop is the planned exit and this trade never ran far enough to sell, so the stop did its job.

deeper.counter: The same trade with the stop moved to breakeven at 2R would have been a scratch. That is allowed, ideally anywhere from 2R to 5R. It is a choice to give back less, not proof that the buy was wrong. MRVL, May 2026: bought at 175.81, best 2.35R, stopped on day 3 at a low of 165.10.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, breakeven window)
+2 held owner question: should breakeven at 2R be the default?

questions.q: Why did this trade end in a loss?
questions.story: A 101% pole, then a 15-day flag 8.5% deep. It breaks out on 1.48x volume, reaches 1.66R, then stalls. On day 7 it trades through your stop.
choices: A valid flag simply failed
The stop was set too tight
The first trim came too late
The pole was too small
questions.why: A valid flag simply failed. IBD: high tight flags are high-risk bases, and many fail. It reached 1.66R, stalled and was stopped on day 7, so the loss stayed at the risk you set when you sized from the stop. The pole more than doubled, so the setup was valid.
questions.lesson_line: Not every good setup works. The stop is what makes that fine.

wrong.The pole was too small: The pole more than doubled. The setup was valid.
wrong.The stop was set too tight: Our stop sits a few cents under the day's low. A wider stop means fewer shares, not a setup that works.
wrong.The first trim came too late: The first trim is a third at 3R, and this trade topped out at 1.66R.

questions.simple: A valid flag simply failed, and the stop kept the loss to the risk you chose.

deeper.trap: Treating a failure as an error. Reaching 1.66R and then stalling is a normal path for a flag that fails. IBD warns that many fail, so the stop and the size do the real work. Changing the rules after one stop-out would not have saved this trade. MDB, June 2023: best 1.66R, stopped on day 7.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4; the stop sets the size)

questions.q: Take the breakout or pass?
questions.story: A 123% pole, then a 16-day flag 17.2% deep. Volume in the flag runs 1.27x the pole's average.
choices: Pass; supply is coming in
Take it; the pole is big
Take it at half size
Pass; flag is too deep
questions.why: Pass. Flag volume ran 1.27x the pole's average. Our card ends the setup when flag volume runs above the pole's average, because supply is coming in, not drying up. IBD: volume generally dries up in a good flag. PDD, December 2020, had a 123% pole and a 17.2% flag, yet best 0.0R, stopped.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume in the flag is somebody selling. Wait for quiet.

wrong.Take it; the pole is big: A huge pole does not cancel heavy selling in the flag.
wrong.Take it at half size: Rising flag volume ends the setup. It is not a size cue.
wrong.Pass; flag is too deep: A flag 17.2% deep is inside IBD's usual 10% to 20%. Depth is not the failed line; volume is.

questions.simple: Pass, because flag volume ran heavier than the pole's, which means supply is coming in, not drying up.

deeper.trap: The trap is the huge pole. A 123% pole feels like proof, but it only shows the stock can run. The flag shows who is selling. PDD's flag volume ran 1.27x the pole's average, and the trade reached 0.0R at best before it was stopped.

reasons: rests on one card line (c17) plus our own dossier example
the flag depth band is a held decision (D-050), but 17.2% is inside every band

questions.q: High tight flag, or something else?
questions.story: A 99% pole, then a 24-day flag 12.7% deep on light volume. Five closes in the flag sit under the 21-day EMA.
choices: A flat base or a cup
A high tight flag
A bull flag
questions.answer: A flat base or a cup
questions.why: A flat base or a cup. Five flag closes sat under the 21-day EMA. A base that lost the fast averages is a flat base or a cup, not a high tight flag.
questions.lesson_line: A real flag rides its fast averages. Lose them and it is a different base.

wrong.A high tight flag: The flag should hold the 21-day EMA. Five closes under it fail that line.
wrong.A bull flag: Measure the pole: a bull flag follows a 20% to 30% run, not a near-double.

questions.q: Which grades higher on volume?
questions.story: Two flags after a double. Flag A trades 45% of the pole's average volume. Flag B trades 95% of it.
choices: Flag A, the quieter flag
Flag B, the busier flag
The same; both pass the gate
Neither; both fail the gate
questions.why: Flag A. Both pass the gate, because flag volume below the pole's average is required. Flag A trades 45% of the pole's average, so it earns the A grade, which is flag volume at most 60% of the pole's. Flag B trades 95%, a B on that line. CRNC's flag volume was 0.95x the pole's, barely under it: a B on that line.
questions.lesson_line: Both pass the gate. The quieter flag earns the higher grade.

wrong.Flag B, the busier flag: Heavier flag volume is less drying up. It passes the gate but grades lower.
wrong.The same; both pass the gate: Passing the gate is not the same grade. The card grades the lighter flag higher.
wrong.Neither; both fail the gate: Both sit below the pole's average, so both pass. The 60% line is only the A grade.

questions.simple: Flag A, because quieter flag volume earns a higher grade, and only Flag A is at 60% or less of the pole's.

deeper.trap: The trap is stopping at the gate. Both flags pass it, so it is easy to call them equal. The card grades by how quiet the flag is, and 60% or less of the pole's volume is the A. CRNC's flag ran at 0.95x the pole's and got a B on this line.

reasons: the 60% A-grade line is a card proposal that can change
rests on one card line (c08)

questions.q: Which context grades higher?
questions.story: Two stocks double in seven weeks. One runs on a news story with no earnings behind it. The other runs on a big earnings beat on heavy volume.
choices: The earnings beat
The news story
They grade the same
Neither can be traded
questions.why: The earnings beat. A real change behind the pole (earnings, a product, a contract) with heavy volume is the A+ context. A news-only story with no earnings is B-. Growth or a real catalyst is preferred, not required, and the chart comes first. Bonde: weigh the earnings and whether it is the first base.
questions.lesson_line: Ask why it doubled. Earnings beat a headline.

wrong.The news story: A news-only story with no earnings is B- context on our card.
wrong.They grade the same: The pole's cause is a grade cue. A real change grades higher.
wrong.Neither can be traded: Earnings are preferred, not required. A news-only story is graded B-, not banned.

questions.simple: The earnings beat grades higher, because a real change in the business with heavy volume beats a story with no earnings.

deeper.counter: A news-only pole is not banned. It is graded B-, and the chart still comes first. Bonde: weigh the earnings and whether it is the first base. Seven of the ten examples in our scan had a report inside the pole, so earnings are the usual cause, not the only one.

reasons: +2 held decision D-007 and proposed card grades (A+ versus B-)
+2 the grades are the card's proposal, not an owner ruling

questions.q: Buy the break?
questions.story: A fast pole, then a flag of eight sessions, 18% deep. At the pattern high, price sits 11% above the 10-day average.
choices: Pass; it is too stretched
Pass; the flag is too deep
Buy; it is clearing the high
Buy with a wider stop for room
questions.why: Pass. We skip a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average, and this one sits 11% above. That holds even at the pattern high. The break is real, and the 18% flag depth is within IBD's usual 10% to 20%. The stretch rule still wins.
questions.lesson_line: A clean break can still be too stretched. Over 10% above the 10-day, we pass.

wrong.Buy; it is clearing the high: The break is real, but the stretch rule says skip it.
wrong.Pass; the flag is too deep: At 18% the flag sits inside IBD's usual 10% to 20%. Depth does not stop this buy. The stretch does.
wrong.Buy with a wider stop for room: A wider stop does not fix a stretched entry.

questions.simple: Pass, because the price is 11% over its 10-day average and our limit is 10%.

deeper.trap: Two separate rules. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average. A buy at the pattern high can pass the first and still fail the second.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C29)
fixed before

questions.q: By our rule, what about the last third?
questions.story: Two weeks after the breakout, the stock gaps up three days running on rising volume. You have already sold two thirds.
choices: Sell a big part into the burst
Hold it all for the trail
Add on strength; it works
Move the stop to the flag low
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the burst
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. For a climax run on your own long, our rule is to sell a big part into it, and it is a judgment call. These breakouts often go vertical. Bulkowski: these rockets go up fast and can return to earth just as quickly. The rest stays on the trail, and we never add.
questions.lesson_line: When it goes vertical, sell into the buyers. Do not wait for the trail.

wrong.Hold it all for the trail: Our rule for a climax run on a long you own is to sell a big part into it. The trail handles the rest.
wrong.Add on strength; it works: We never add. The full size went on at one price.
wrong.Move the stop to the flag low: The stop only moves up, and the flag low is far below.

questions.simple: Sell a big part into the burst, because these breakouts often go straight up and can fall back just as fast.

deeper.trap: Waiting for the trail. The trail is a close below the 10-day or 21-day average, so it sells after the burst has turned, not into it. A climax run can fall back as fast as it rose. The rule asks you to sell a big part into the burst, and it is a judgment call.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C34, a judgment call)

questions.q: What gets you out of the rest of the position?
questions.story: Bought at 264.95, stop 255.06. You sold part into the push and the rest still rides. It ran to about 354 and now turns down hard.
choices: A close below the trail average
A close under the flag low itself
A close back down at your 3R price
Nothing; hold on for a double
questions.answer: A close below the trail average
questions.why: A close below the trailing average. After you sell into the push, what is left rides the trail: sell on a close below it. The default trail is the 10-day average for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones. BIDU went to about 354 in three weeks, then collapsed under the flag low by late March. The trail is what gets you out.
questions.lesson_line: These rockets come back as fast as they went up. The trail is your exit.

wrong.A close under the flag low itself: By then most of the run is gone. BIDU fell under it by late March.
wrong.A close back down at your 3R price: That is not an exit rule. What is left rides the trail.
wrong.Nothing; hold on for a double: Holding for more is not an exit rule. Bulkowski: these rockets go up fast and can return to earth just as quickly.

questions.simple: A close below the trailing average gets you out of the rest before a fast run unwinds.

deeper.example: BIDU, February 2021. Bought at 264.95, stop 255.06. It reached 3R on day 2 and 5R after that. It ran to about 354 within three weeks, then collapsed under the flag low by late March. The trail is what gets you out of what is left.

reasons: +2 held decision D-024 (which average is the trail)

questions.q: In our scan of 54 hits, most reached 3R before the stop.
questions.why: False. 16 of 54 hits (29.6%) reached 3R before the stop, and 12 of 54 (22.2%) reached 5R, on a fixed stop with no trims. IBD: high tight flags are high-risk bases, and many fail.
questions.lesson_line: Most hits stall before 3R. The stop and the size do the real work.
questions.simple: False, because only 29.6% of the 54 hits in our scan reached 3R before the stop.

deeper.trap: A base rate is not a forecast. In our own scan of 54 hits on a fixed stop with no trims, 29.6% reached 3R and 22.2% reached 5R. Read what a statistic measured before you lean on it.

reasons: +2 rests on our own scan (d23), a Tier 3 fact
+1 the scan figures change with the data

questions.q: A reader tested these with a mechanical scan. What was Bonde's reply?
choices: Late flags fail; context decides
The scan is right; avoid them all
Trade the scan as a mechanical system
Early flags fail; late flags work
questions.why: Late flags fail; context decides. Bonde: if a tight flag appears late in the move, it will break down. He adds that you must weigh the earnings and whether it is the first base. He says it cannot be traded as a mechanical system, because the interpretation becomes critical. Our not-late test applies this: the pole must be the first or second big leg.
questions.lesson_line: The pattern is the start. The context decides whether it is ours.

wrong.The scan is right; avoid them all: Bonde did not drop the pattern. He called it rare but very profitable and said the reading becomes critical.
wrong.Trade the scan as a mechanical system: Bonde said the opposite: it cannot be traded as a mechanical system.
wrong.Early flags fail; late flags work: Backwards. Bonde: a tight flag late in the move breaks down.

questions.simple: Bonde said late flags tend to fail, so you must judge the context, since it cannot be traded as a mechanical system.

deeper.trap: The trap is trusting the scan. A scan can find 'doubled, then tight' mechanically, but it cannot see where the flag sits in the move. Bonde's two checks are the earnings and whether it is the first base. Our card turns the second into a gate: the pole is the first or second big leg.

reasons: all three quotes come from one Bonde post (single source)
the reader's scan is described only on that page

questions.q: You are up 3.5R and a report lands later this week. Hold through it?
choices: Sell it all before the report
Sell half and hold the rest
Hold it; a 3.5R winner has cushion
Hold it, with the stop at breakeven
questions.answer: Sell it all before the report
questions.why: Sell before it. Hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R. At 3.5R you are short of that line. A tight flag or a breakeven stop does not bend the rule.
questions.lesson_line: Up 5R rides through a report. Anything less, you sell first.

wrong.Sell half and hold the rest: Holding any part through the report breaks the rule. Only a trade up 5R holds through it.
wrong.Hold it; a 3.5R winner has cushion: Being a winner is not enough. The line is 5R.
wrong.Hold it, with the stop at breakeven: A stop at breakeven is allowed from 2R. It does not lift the trade to the 5R line.

questions.simple: Sell it. Hold through a report only if up 5R, and 3.5R is short of that line.

deeper.trap: Judge the cushion in R, not by the chart. A third may be off and the stop at breakeven, yet the report rule still says sell. Only 5R carries a trade through.

reasons: one cited fact only
rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: Buy it again?
questions.story: You were stopped out the day after a breakout. Two weeks later the stock builds a fresh tight flag, meets every test again and trades through its high.
choices: Yes, as a new trade, new stop
No; it already failed once
Yes, at double size to recover
No; wait a full month first
questions.answer: Yes, as a new trade, new stop
questions.why: Yes, as a new trade. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule. A fresh tight flag trading through its high is a new trigger when every test is met again. The limit is at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is not a ban. A new trigger is a new trade.

wrong.No; it already failed once: One stop-out does not end the stock. A new trigger is a new trade.
wrong.Yes, at double size to recover: Size comes from the new stop and our risk, never from making it back.
wrong.No; wait a full month first: No rule sets a waiting period. After a stop-out we buy again on a new trigger, as a new trade.

questions.simple: Yes, if the setup triggers again, because a stop-out is not a ban and the new trade gets its own stop.

deeper.trap: Revenge. After a stop-out the pull is to win it back with more size or the old stop. A new trigger is a new trade: its own stop under the new day's low, its size from that stop, and every rule again. The cap is 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B21 and E56)

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before a breakout. Take it or pass?
choices: Take it; the pole doubled
Take it; flag volume is rising
Pass; the run is far too small
Pass; the flag is far too deep
questions.why: Take it. The pole was +129% in 14 sessions, a real double. The flag ran 14 days sideways, 15.0% deep. IBD says a flag usually pulls back 10% to 20%. Flag volume was 0.66x the pole's, so it was drying up.
questions.lesson_line: Count the pole first. A real double, then a quiet shelf: that is the setup.

wrong.Pass; the run is far too small: Look at the run in front of the shelf: well over a double, in weeks.
wrong.Pass; the flag is far too deep: The flag gave back 15.0% of price, a normal depth for this pattern. IBD: usually 10% to 20%.
wrong.Take it; flag volume is rising: Flag volume ran at 0.66x the pole's: drying up, not rising. IBD: volume generally dries up in the flag.

questions.simple: Take it, because the stock more than doubled in a few weeks and then rested in a flag of normal depth.

deeper.example: SRPT, June 2015. A report on 2015-05-07, then a +60% day on 2015-05-20 topped a near-vertical two-week run. A 14-day sideways flag held the 21-day EMA. Bought at 27.50 with the stop at 26.59, it reached 3R on day 5. Count the pole first, then judge the shelf.

reasons: +2 the figures are read off our own daily bars and can change

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before it trades through a tight flag's high. Weigh the last 8 weeks. Take it as a high tight flag, or pass?
choices: Pass; the run never doubled
Take it; the flag is tight
Take it; it is a strong leader
Pass; flag volume is too heavy
questions.why: Pass. The pole was +78% in 40 sessions; the rule asks for 90% or more. A tight flag in a leader that never doubled is a bull flag, however tight. The flag itself was tight, 8 days and 6.7% deep on 0.78x volume, but the pole decides the setup. Best 1.88R, stopped.
questions.lesson_line: Tight is not enough. No double, no high tight flag.

wrong.Take it; the flag is tight: The flag is tight, and that is all. The pole decides the setup.
wrong.Take it; it is a strong leader: Leaders make bull flags too. The rule asks for a pole of 90% or more.
wrong.Pass; flag volume is too heavy: Flag volume ran at 0.78x the pole's: lighter, not heavier. The flag was fine; the pole is what failed.

questions.simple: Pass, because the pole was only 78% in 40 sessions, and a tight flag after a smaller run is a bull flag.

deeper.counter: Tight is not wrong, it is just not enough. This flag was a clean 8 days, 6.7% deep, on 0.78x volume, and it still reached only 1.88R before it was stopped. A bull flag has its own card. The question here is which card applies, and the pole answers it.

reasons: +2 held decision D-048 (how big the pole must be)
+2 the figures are read off our own daily bars

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On our card, the pole's rise takes ___ sessions or fewer.
questions.why: 40. Our card wants the rise done in 40 sessions, about 8 weeks. IBD describes a span of four to eight weeks. Bulkowski allows 2 months or less. The sources agree the rise is fast: eight weeks, or about two months at most.
questions.lesson_line: The pole is fast: 40 sessions or fewer, about 8 weeks.
questions.simple: 40, because our card wants the rise done in 40 sessions, which is about 8 weeks.

reasons: a number that can change (40 sessions) set by our card, with IBD and Bulkowski giving slightly different spans

questions.q: Which test does the pole fail?
questions.story: A leader rose 110% over 14 weeks, off a quiet base, after an earnings beat. Since then it has rested tight just under the high.
choices: The time test: too many weeks
The size test: too small
The base test: not quiet
The cause test: no change

wrong.The size test: too small: A rise of 110% is a double and clears the size test.
wrong.The base test: not quiet: The story says it rose off a quiet base, so that test passes.
wrong.The cause test: no change: An earnings beat is a real change, so that test passes.

questions.answer: The time test: too many weeks
questions.why: The time test. Our card wants the rise done in 40 sessions or fewer, about 8 weeks. This pole took 14 weeks, far past that, so it is no pole even though it rose 110%. IBD describes four to eight weeks, and Bulkowski 2 months or less. The size, the quiet base and the earnings beat all pass.
questions.lesson_line: A double over 14 weeks is not a pole. Speed is part of the pattern.
questions.simple: The time test, because the card wants the rise done in 40 sessions, about 8 weeks, and 14 weeks is far longer.

deeper.trap: The trap is the double. A rise of 110% is more than a double, so the size test passes and the eye stops there. The pole must also be fast: the rise takes 40 sessions or fewer, about 8 weeks. Over 14 weeks it is a slow climb, not a pole.

reasons: a number that can change (40 sessions) set by our card, backed by IBD and Bulkowski

questions.q: On our card, the close is above the 50-day average at the trigger.
questions.why: True. Our card wants the close above the 50-day simple moving average at the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: At the trigger, the close is above the 50-day average.
questions.simple: True, because our card wants the close above the 50-day average at the trigger.

reasons: rests on the card only (single source, c49)

questions.q: On our card, price is above a rising 10-day and a rising 21-day EMA at the trigger.
questions.why: True. At the trigger the card wants price above a rising 10-day and a rising 21-day EMA. Kullamagi describes the same ride: during the consolidation the stock surfs the rising 10- and 20-day averages. Our card uses the 21-day.
questions.lesson_line: Price should ride rising fast averages into the trigger.
questions.simple: True, because our card wants price above both fast averages, and both rising, when the stock triggers.

reasons: +2 the 21-day EMA line is the card's proposal, not an owner ruling

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A base that lost the fast averages is a flat base or a ___, not a high tight flag.
questions.why: Cup. A base that lost the fast averages is a flat base or a cup, not a high tight flag. The flag must keep riding them.
questions.lesson_line: Lose the fast averages and it is a base, not a flag.

questions.q: Which tightness cue marks the A+ flag on our card?
choices: Weekly closes bunched together
Narrow daily ranges every bar
Light volume on each flag day
A gap up through the flag top

wrong.Narrow daily ranges every bar: IBD's JDSU flag had wide weekly ranges and still had tight closes. Closes are the cue.
wrong.Light volume on each flag day: Flag volume has its own line: at most 60% of the pole's is the A grade. It is not the tightness cue.
